source.title: Fluent dreaming for language models
source.authors: T. Thompson; Zygimantas Straznickas; Michael Sklar

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures optimized inputs that activate language-model neurons and reports whether the responses appear polysemantic, using EPO rather than the original vision-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper examines six Pythia-12B neurons, but gives detailed polysemanticity analysis for L10.N5 and L3.N1000. Table 3's single maximum-activating prompt per neuron does not by itself show whether a neuron responds to unrelated inputs. Residual-stream alignment and token-logit results do not measure neuron polysemanticity and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a methods paper (EPO). Its qualitative analysis of two Pythia-12B MLP neurons still reports whether they respond to unrelated inputs, and how this depends on activation range. That bears on V2 for single neurons and on V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors present EPO as the first successful fluent dreaming method for language models, valuable for exploring out-of-distribution behaviour. They caution that max-activating prompts can mislead, and they note L10.N5 is polysemantic below activation 5 while L3.N1000 is polysemantic even at top activations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses discrete token-space Evolutionary Prompt Optimization, extending GCG with a fluency objective and a population spanning a Pareto frontier; it does not use the original vision-model dreaming procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: For Pythia-12B-L10.N5, the interpretation depends on the activation range examined: activations above 5 are usually associated with example-related phrases, while the authors describe polysemanticity at activations up to 5. EPO results also vary across random initializations, as reported for L10.N5.
record.problems: Only six neurons were examined, with detailed qualitative analysis focused on two; the paper does not estimate prevalence across neurons. Interpretations of response categories are qualitative, and the authors note that EPO can get stuck in local minima and that results vary across random initializations.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 and Appendix Table 5 report additional optimized prompts and activations for six neurons, but a single prompt or further prompts without a reported result bearing on response diversity were not entered as separate rows. Residual-stream and token-logit experiments do not test the claim versions about neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: The share of polysemantic MLP neurons, comparisons across layers, and models other than Pythia-12B. Only two neurons are analysed for polysemanticity.
Causes of polysemanticity, superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or training noise.
Effects of architecture, activation function or regularization.
Whether apparently unrelated responses share one feature, and how rare truly unrelated mixtures are.
Explanation-scoring methods. Activation-range dependence is shown for one neuron only, qualitatively.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper; the polysemanticity evidence is incidental and qualitative, with no counts or blind labelling. Table 5 shows Pareto prompts for six neurons, some with seemingly distinct prompt families (e.g. L17.N3), but the authors make no polysemanticity claims about them, so they are rightly left out. The text cites Elhage 2022 and Gurnee 2023 for neurons being frequently polysemantic; that is a cited result, not a finding of this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not estimate the share of MLP neurons that are polysemantic, compare layers systematically, or study transformer models beyond Pythia-12B.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Effects of activation function, architecture, regularization, or performance-preserving reductions in polysemanticity.
Whether apparently unrelated responses are actually a shared feature or related offshoots, and how frequently genuinely unrelated mixtures occur.
The study does not compare explanation-scoring methods; it discusses activation ranges and gives a qualitative interpretation.

rows.subject: Pythia-12B-L10.N5
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron activations for EPO-generated prompts and interpreted the prompts by activation range.
rows.measure: Neuron activation and the semantic type of prompts that produce it
rows.value: The authors report that activations above 5 seem to be almost always triggered by example-related phrases.
rows.note: The authors distinguish this higher-activation range from prompts producing activations up to 5.
rows.check: Taken alone this row shows near-monosemantic behaviour above activation 5. It bears on V7 only together with R2, which shows the range dependence.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, lines 391-393; Table 4 (all listed prompts have activations above 5)

rows.subject: Pythia-12B-L10.N5
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron activations for EPO-generated prompts and interpreted the prompts by activation range.
rows.measure: Neuron activation and the authors' characterization of response diversity
rows.value: The authors state that many prompts produce activations up to 5 and characterize the neuron as polysemantic when those lower activations are considered.
rows.note: The paper does not enumerate these prompts or give a count of unrelated response categories for this range.
rows.check: For V2, polysemanticity appears only below activation 5. The paper does not list the lower-range prompts or say what unrelated inputs they contain, so the evidence is an assertion without examples.

rows.subject: Pythia-12B-L3.N1000
rows.operation_detail: Applied EPO to find prompts activating the neuron and qualitatively interpreted the responses.
rows.measure: Neuron activation and semantic diversity of activating prompts
rows.value: The authors report polysemanticity even among the highest activations, describing responses to component-related words, list items, and the word “depending”; they say the behavior is not easily decipherable.
rows.note: The paper presents these as several possible response types, without quantifying their prevalence.
rows.check: This is one neuron with qualitative categories only: component words, list items, and 'depending'. The authors themselves call it 'not easily decipherable'.

relationships.reason: The neuron responds to apparently unrelated triggers even at its highest activations (R3). This is qualitative and covers one neuron.
relationships.display_finding: Neuron L3.N1000 responded to apparently unrelated triggers even at its peak activations. The evidence is qualitative and covers a single neuron.

tranche.reason: It uses a different method (EPO dreaming rather than dataset examples) and reports qualitative neuron analyses that bear on polysemanticity.

source_check.notes: The L10.N5 range dependence is the authors' qualitative assertion about one neuron. All prompts in Table 4 have activations above 5, and no lower-range prompts are shown. Only the top (dreamed) range of L3.N1000 is examined, which is why R3 bears on V2 only.
